\label{rem:rate}
	The proof provides an admissible choice of the decay rate in
	\eqref{1.11a}. More precisely, fix
	\(r\in(0,\min\{1,\alpha/2\})\), and let \(\lambda>0\) be the
	decay rate furnished by Lemma~\ref{lemma4.4}. Then, for any
	$
	0<\mu<\frac12\min\{2a,(\alpha-2r)\lambda\}$,	one may choose
	\(\eta_p=\mu\) when \(1\le p<2\) and
	\(\eta_p=2\mu/p\) when \(2\le p<\infty\).

label: rem:macroscopic
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:macroscopic}
Theorem~\ref{theorem1.2} excludes persistent macroscopic patterns only in the following sense: since \(u(\cdot,t)\to a/b\) in \(L^p(\Omega)\) for every \(1\le p<\infty\), any \(O(1)\)-amplitude non-uniformity must be supported on sets of vanishing measure. However, small-measure heterogeneities are not excluded, and strong \(L^\infty\)-convergence remains open.

(\cite[Theorem~1.2]{Wang2025})\label{pro1.1}
	Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ be a bounded domain with smooth boundary. Assume that $\alpha\geq 1$, $\phi$
 satisfies \eqref{1.5}--\eqref{1.6}, and $(u_0,v_0)$ fulfills \eqref{1.8}. Then for $a>0$ and $b>0$,  problem \eqref{1.1} admits
  a  classical solution  $(u,v)\in (C^0(\overline\Omega\times [0,\infty))\cap  C^{2,1}(\overline\Omega \times (0,\infty)))^2$, where $u(x,t)>0$ and $v(x,t)>0$ for all $x\in \overline \Omega$ and $t>0$.

label: le3.1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{le3.1}
	Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^2$ be  a smoothly bounded domain, and suppose that $p>2$, $\alpha>0$ and $1< r<\infty$. Then for any $\eta>0$ one can find a constant $C(\eta,p,r,\alpha,\Omega)>0$
		such that
		\begin{align}\label{3.1}
			\|\varphi^{\frac{p}{2}}\psi^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}\|^2_{L^{r}(\Omega)}\leq \eta \int_{\Omega}\varphi^{p-2}\psi^\alpha|\nabla \varphi|^2+\eta
			\int_{\Omega}\varphi^{p}\psi^{\alpha-2}|\nabla \psi|^2+C(\eta, p,r,\alpha,\Omega)\cdot
			\left\{\int_{\Omega}\varphi\right\}^{p}\left\{\sup\limits_{x\in\Omega}\psi(x)\right\}^\alpha
		\end{align}for all $\varphi, \psi\in C^1(\overline{\Omega})$  with $\varphi,\psi>0$ in $\overline{\Omega}$.

label: le3.2
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It is observed that the restriction $q>2+\frac{2p}{p_0}$ ensures that $\frac{pq}{q-2}<p+p_0$.
	Firstly, we verify this lemma in the case
	\begin{equation}\label{3.6}
		\beta \in \left[\frac{pq}{q-2},p+p_0\right).
	\end{equation}
	Let
	$$\rho:=\frac{p_0}{p_0-\beta+p}\quad and \quad \rho_*:=\frac{p_0}{\beta-p}.$$
	Due to \eqref{3.6}, it follows that
	$
		\rho>1$ and $\rho_*>1.
	$
	Thanks to  $\int_{\Omega}\varphi^{p_0}\leq L$, the H\"{o}lder inequality, the Young inequality and Lemma \ref{le3.1},  we conclude that for any $\eta>0$, there exist
	positive constants  $c_1=c_1(\eta,p,\beta,L)$ and $c_2=c_2(\eta,p,q)$  such that
	\begin{align*}
		\int_{\Omega}\varphi^{\beta}\psi^\alpha&=\int_{\Omega}(\varphi^{\frac{p}{2}}\psi^{\frac{\alpha}{2}})^2\varphi^{\beta-p}\nonumber
		\\
		&\leq\|\varphi^{\frac{p}{2}}\psi^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}\|^2_{L^{2\rho}(\Omega)}\cdot\|\varphi^{\beta-p}\|_{L^{\rho_*}(\Omega)}\nonumber
		\\
		&=\|\varphi^{\frac{p}{2}}\psi^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}\|^2_{L^{2\rho}(\Omega)}
		\cdot\|\varphi\|_{L^{p_0}(\Omega)}^{\beta-p}\nonumber
		\\
		&\leq L^{\frac {\beta-p}{p_0}}\|\varphi^{\frac{p}{2}}\psi^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}\|^2_{L^{2\rho}(\Omega)}\nonumber
		\\
		&\leq \frac{\eta}{2}\int_{\Omega}\varphi^{p-2}\psi^\alpha|\nabla
		\varphi|^2
+\frac{\eta}{2}\int_{\Omega}\varphi^{p}\psi^{\alpha-2}|\nabla\psi|^2
+c_1\left\{\int_{\Omega}\varphi\right\}^{p}\cdot
\left\{\sup\limits_{x\in\Omega}\psi(x)\right\}^\alpha\nonumber
		\\
		&\leq \frac{\eta}{2}\int_{\Omega}\varphi^{p-2}\psi^\alpha|\nabla
		\varphi|^2+\frac{\eta}{2}\int_{\Omega}\varphi\frac{|\nabla
			\psi|^q}{\psi^{q-1}}+\frac {\eta}2\int_{\Omega}\varphi^{\frac{qp-2}{q-2}}\psi^{\frac{\alpha q-2}{q-2}}+c_1\left\{\int_{\Omega}\varphi\right\}^{p}
\left\{\sup\limits_{x\in\Omega}\psi(x)\right\}^\alpha\nonumber
		\\
			&\leq \frac{\eta}{2}\int_{\Omega}\varphi^{p-2}\psi^\alpha|\nabla
		\varphi|^2+\frac{\eta}{2}\int_{\Omega}\varphi\frac{|\nabla
			\psi|^q}{\psi^{q-1}}+\frac {\eta}2\left\{\sup\limits_{x\in\Omega}\psi(x)\right\}^{\frac{2(\alpha-1)}{q-2}}\int_{\Omega}\varphi^{\frac{qp-2}{q-2}}\psi^\alpha\\
			&\quad+c_1\left\{\int_{\Omega}\varphi\right\}^{p}
\left\{\sup\limits_{x\in\Omega}\psi(x)\right\}^\alpha\nonumber
		\\
		&\leq \frac{\eta}{2}\int_{\Omega}\varphi^{p-2}\psi^\alpha|\nabla
		\varphi|^2+\frac{\eta}{2}\int_{\Omega}\varphi\frac{|\nabla
			\psi|^q}{\psi^{q-1}}+
		\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}\varphi^{\beta}\psi^\alpha
+c_2\left\{\sup\limits_{x\in\Omega}\psi(x)\right\}^{\frac{2(\alpha-1) (\beta-1)}{(q-2)(\beta-\frac{qp-2}{q-2})}}\int_{\Omega}\varphi\psi^\alpha\\
		&\quad+c_1\left\{\int_{\Omega}\varphi\right\}^{p}
\left\{\sup\limits_{x\in\Omega}\psi(x)\right\}^\alpha\\
		&\leq \frac{\eta}{2}\int_{\Omega}\varphi^{p-2}\psi^\alpha|\nabla
		\varphi|^2+\frac{\eta}{2}\int_{\Omega}\varphi\frac{|\nabla
			\psi|^q}{\psi^{q-1}}+
		\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}\varphi^{\beta}\psi^\alpha
+c_2\left\{\sup\limits_{x\in\Omega}\psi(x)+1\right\}^\frac{\alpha q(\beta-p)-2(\beta-1)}{(q-2)\beta-(qp-2)}\int_{\Omega}\varphi\\
		&\quad+c_1\left\{\int_{\Omega}\varphi\right\}^{p}
\left\{\sup\limits_{x\in\Omega}\psi(x)+1\right\}^\alpha
	\end{align*}
	and thus
	\begin{align}\label{3.7}
		\int_{\Omega}\varphi^{\beta}\psi^\alpha&\leq \eta\int_{\Omega}\varphi^{p-2}\psi^\alpha|\nabla
		\varphi|^2+\eta\int_{\Omega}\varphi{\psi}^{-q+1}|\nabla  \psi|^q\nonumber\\
		&\quad+c_3\left\{\sup\limits_{x\in\Omega}\psi(x)+1\right\}^\tau\left\{\int_{\Omega}\varphi
+\left\{\int_{\Omega}\varphi\right\}^{p}\right\}
		                                                                                                                        
	\end{align}
	                                                                                                                                                                
with
$$\tau:=\frac{ pq(\alpha-1)}{q-2}+1=\sup_{\beta\in\left[\frac{pq}{q-2},p+p_0\right)}\big\{\frac{\alpha q(\beta-p)-2(\beta-1)}{(q-2)\beta-(qp-2)}\big\}.
$$
	Furthermore, it is observed that  for $\beta \in [1, \frac{qp}{q-2})$, there exists $c_4=c_4(p,q)>0$ such that $$\int_{\Omega}\varphi^{\beta}\psi^\alpha\leq
	\int_{\Omega}\varphi^{\frac{qp}{q-2}}\psi^\alpha+c_4\int_{\Omega}\varphi\psi^\alpha $$
by the Young inequality. 	The latter along with \eqref{3.7}  completes the proof readily.

Lemma~\ref{le3.2} is the key tool for handling the cross-diffusive term $\phi'(v)u^{p-1}\nabla v\cdot\nabla u$: it enables us to control the mixed integral $\int_\Omega u^\beta v^\alpha$ by the available $u$-related dissipation and the weighted gradient dissipation of $v$ from Lemma~\ref{lemma3.3},
  with parameters chosen precisely to match the degenerate structure.

title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{2.2} and \eqref{1.6}, there exist positive constants $c_1$ and $c_2$ such that
	\begin{equation}\label{4.4}
		c_1 v^{\alpha}(x,t)\leq\phi(v(x,t))~~\mbox{and}~|\phi'(v(x,t))|\leq c_2 v^{\alpha-1}(x,t)~~\mbox{for}~(x,t)\in\Omega\times(0,\infty).
	\end{equation}
	
Set $u_*:=\frac ab$. Due to $u>0$,  testing the $u$-equation in \eqref{1.1} by
	$(u-u_*)/u$  and integrating by parts, we obtain
  that
	\begin{align}\label{4.5}
			\frac{d}{dt}\int_\Omega(u-u_*-u_*\ln\frac{u}{u_*})
			&=\int_\Omega\Delta(\phi(v)u)\frac{u-u_*}{u}+a\int_\Omega(u-u_*)-b\int_\Omega u(u-u_*)\nonumber\\
			                                                                                                      
			&=-\int_\Omega\frac{|\nabla u|^2u_*}{u^2}\phi(v)-\int_\Omega\frac{u_*}{u}\phi'(v)\nabla v\cdot\nabla u-b\int_\Omega(u-u_*)^2\\
			&\leq-\frac{1}{2}\int_\Omega\frac{|\nabla u|^2u_*}{u^2}\phi(v)+\frac{1}{2}\int_\Omega\frac{|\phi'(v)|^2u_*}{\phi(v)}|\nabla v|^2-b\int_\Omega(u-u_*)^2\nonumber\\
			&\leq\frac{c_2^2u_*}{2c_1}\int_\Omega v^{\alpha-2}|\nabla v|^2 -b\int_\Omega(u-u_*)^2.\nonumber
	\end{align}
	Since  $u-u_*-u_*\ln\frac{u}{u_*}\geq 0$,  integrating \eqref{4.5} from $1$ to $t$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{46f}
		b\int^t_1\int_\Omega(u-u_*)^2\leq  \int_\Omega (u(\cdot,1)-u_*-u_*\ln\frac{u(\cdot,1)}{u_*})+
		\frac{c_2^2u_*}{2c_1}   \int^t_1\int_\Omega v^{\alpha-2}|\nabla v|^2.
	\end{equation}
	Letting $t\to\infty$ in  \eqref{46f} and using \eqref{4.1}, we deduce \eqref{4.2}.

To prove \eqref{4.3}, we first observe from \eqref{4.5} and \eqref{4.1} that
	\[
		\int_\Omega\left(u(\cdot,t)-u_*-u_*\ln\frac{u(\cdot,t)}{u_*}\right)
		\leq c_3
		\qquad\mbox{for all }t>1,
	\]
	where
	\[
		c_3:=\int_\Omega\left(u(\cdot,1)-u_*-u_*\ln\frac{u(\cdot,1)}{u_*}\right)
		+\frac{c_2^2u_*}{2c_1}\int_1^\infty\int_\Omega v^{\alpha-2}|\nabla v|^2.
	\]
	Hence, for every $t>1$,
	\begin{align*}
		\int_\Omega\ln\frac{u(\cdot,t)}{u_*}
		\geq -|\Omega|-\frac{c_3}{u_*}=:c_4
	\end{align*}
	So Jensen's inequality yields	$
	\int_\Omega u(\cdot,t)=\frac{a}b \int_\Omega e^{\ln \frac{u(\cdot,t)}{u_*}}\geq \frac {a|\Omega|}b e^{\frac{c_4}{|\Omega|}}
	=:\kappa$ for all $t>1$.

label: lemma4.3
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set
	\begin{equation}\label{4.8}
		y(t):=\frac12\int_\Omega\left(u(\cdot,t)-\frac{a}{b}\right)^2,
		\qquad
		h(t):=\int_\Omega v^{\alpha-2}|\nabla v|^2.
	\end{equation}
	Testing the first equation in \eqref{1.1} with $u-a/b$ and integrating by
	parts, we obtain
	\begin{align}\label{4.9}
		y'(t)
		&=-\int_\Omega\phi(v)|\nabla u|^2
		-\int_\Omega u\phi'(v)\nabla u\cdot\nabla v
		-b\int_\Omega u\left(u-\frac{a}{b}\right)^2.
	\end{align}
	By Young's inequality, Theorem
	\ref{theorem1.1} and \eqref{4.4}, there exists a constant $C>0$ such that
	\begin{align*}
		-\int_\Omega u\phi'(v)\nabla u\cdot\nabla v
		&\leq \frac12\int_\Omega\phi(v)|\nabla u|^2
		+\frac12\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}^2
		\int_\Omega\frac{|\phi'(v)|^2}{\phi(v)}|\nabla v|^2\\
		&\leq \frac12\int_\Omega\phi(v)|\nabla u|^2+C h(t),
	\end{align*}
	which along with \eqref{4.9} then entails
\begin{align}\label{4.10}
y'(t)\leq C h(t).
\end{align}	
	From \eqref{4.2},  it follows that $y\in L^1((1,\infty))$  and thereby there is a sequence $t_j\to\infty$ such that
	$y(t_j)\to0$.  Integrating \eqref{4.10} from $t_j$ to $t> t_j$ gives
	$
	y(t)\leq y(t_j)+C\int_{t_j}^{\infty}h(s)\,ds.
	$
Thanks to \eqref{4.1},
	 $\int_{t_j}^{\infty}h(s)\,ds\to 0$ as $t_j\to\infty$ and hence we arrive at
$y(t)\to0 $ as $t\to\infty$, that is,
	\begin{equation}\label{4.5a}
		\|u(\cdot,t)-a/b\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\to0\quad\mbox{as }t\to\infty.
	\end{equation}

title: Proof
body_md:
Testing the second equation in \eqref{1.1} by $v$ yields
\begin{equation}\label{4.13}
\frac12\frac d{dt}\int_\Omega v^2+\int_\Omega|\nabla v|^2+\frac ab\int_\Omega v^2
=-\int_\Omega(u-\frac ab)v^2.
\end{equation}
By H\"{o}lder's inequality and the two-dimensional Gagliardo--Nirenberg
inequality, we have
\begin{align}\label{4.14}
\left|\int_\Omega(u-\frac ab)v^2\right|
\le & C_{GN}\,\varepsilon(t)\,(\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}\|v\|_{L^2}+\|v\|_{L^2}^2)\nonumber\\
\le & \frac{1}{2} \|\nabla v\|_{L^2}^2
+ \Big(\frac{C_{GN}^2 \varepsilon^2(t)}{2}+C_{GN} \varepsilon(t)\Big)\|v\|_{L^2}^2,
\end{align}
with
$\varepsilon(t):=\|u(\cdot,t)-a/b\|_{L^2(\Omega)}$.

By Lemma \ref{lemma4.3}, $\varepsilon(t)\to0$ as $t\to\infty$; hence
there exists $t_0>0$ such that $C_{GN}^2 \varepsilon^2(t)+C_{GN} \varepsilon(t)<\frac a{2b}$ for all
$t>t_0$.
Therefore substituting \eqref{4.14} into \eqref{4.13}, we obtain
  that  for  all $t>t_0$,
$
\frac d{dt}\|v(\cdot,t)\|_{L^2}^2\le-\frac ab\,\|v(\cdot,t)\|_{L^2}^2,
$
which yields the exponential decay of $\|v(\cdot,t)\|_{L^2}$. Furthermore, by Theorem \ref{theorem1.1}, \(\|\nabla v\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\le C\) and hence \(\|\nabla v\|_{L^4(\Omega)}\le C|\Omega|^{1/4}\). According to the two-dimensional
Gagliardo--Nirenberg inequality
\[
\|v\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}
\le C_{GN}\|\nabla v\|_{L^4(\Omega)}^{2/3}
\|v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^{1/3}
+C_{GN}\|v\|_{L^2(\Omega)},
\]
the exponential decay of \(\|v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\) implies that of
\(\|v\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\). Hence combining this with \(\|\nabla v\|_{L^\infty}\le c_1\|v\|_{L^\infty}^{1-r}\) from Lemma \ref{lem3.5}, we arrive at \eqref{4.12} readily.

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $u_*:=a/b$, $s(x,t):=u(x,t)/u_*$, and
	\[
		\Psi(s):=s^{-4}+4s-5,
		\qquad E(t):=\int_\Omega\Psi(s(\cdot,t)).
	\]
	By the positivity of $u(\cdot,t)$ for all $t>0$, the functional $E(t)$ is well defined on $(0,\infty)$.   A direct calculation gives
	\begin{equation}\label{4.16}
		4(s^{-4}-s)(1-s)-2\Psi(s)
		=\frac{2(s-1)^4(2s^2+2s+1)}{s^4}\geq0.
	\end{equation}
	Since $s_t=u_t/u_*$, we get
	\begin{align}\label{4.17}
		E'(t)
		&=\int_\Omega\frac{\Psi'(s)}{u_*}\Delta(\phi(v)u)
		+a\int_\Omega\Psi'(s)s(1-s)\nonumber\\
		&=\int_\Omega\frac{\Psi'(s)}{u_*}\Delta(\phi(v)u)-4a\int_\Omega(s^{-4}-s)(1-s)\\
		&\leq\int_\Omega\frac{\Psi'(s)}{u_*}\Delta(\phi(v)u)-2aE(t)\nonumber
	\end{align}
	by \eqref{4.16}.
	On the other hand, by integration by parts, we have
		\begin{align}
		&\int_\Omega\frac{\Psi'(s)}{u_*}\Delta(\phi(v)u)\nonumber\\
=&-\int_\Omega\frac{\Psi''(s)}{u_*^2}\phi(v)|\nabla u|^2
		-\int_\Omega\frac{\Psi''(s)s}{u_*}\phi'(v)\nabla u\cdot\nabla v\nonumber\\
=&-\int_\Omega\frac{\Psi''(s)\phi(v)}{u_*^2}
		\left|\nabla u+\frac{u_*s\phi'(v)}{2\phi(v)}\nabla v\right|^2+\frac14\int_\Omega\Psi''(s)s^2
		\frac{|\phi'(v)|^2}{\phi(v)}|\nabla v|^2\nonumber\\
\leq& 5\int_\Omega s^{-4}
		\frac{|\phi'(v)|^2}{\phi(v)}|\nabla v|^2.\label{4.18}
	\end{align}
	Fix $r\in(0,\min\{1,\alpha/2\})$, then by assumption \eqref{1.6}, Lemma
	\ref{lem3.5} and Lemma \ref{lemma4.4}, we  can see that there exist $c_i>0$, ($i=1,2$), such that
	\begin{equation}\label{4.19}
		G(t):=\left\|\frac{|\phi'(v(\cdot,t))|^2}{\phi(v(\cdot,t))}
		|\nabla v(\cdot,t)|^2\right\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\leq c_1\left\|v^{\alpha-2}|\nabla v|^2\right\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}
		\leq c_2 e^{-(\alpha-2r)\lambda t}.
	\end{equation}
	Since $\int_\Omega s^{-4}(\cdot,t)\leq E(t)+5|\Omega|$, the combination of  \eqref{4.17}-\eqref{4.19} leads to
	\begin{equation}\label{4.20}
		E'(t)+(2a-5G(t))E(t)\leq25|\Omega|G(t),
	\end{equation}
	and thereby for every fixed  $ \mu_1\in(0,\min\{2a,(\alpha-2r)\lambda\})$  there exists a constant $c_3>0$ such that
	for all $t\geq1$,
\begin{equation}\label{4.21}	E(t)\leq c_3 e^{-\mu_1 t}. \end{equation}

Furthermore, by Theorem~\ref{theorem1.1},
$
\sup_{t>0}\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}<\infty$.
 We therefore set
\[
M:=\max\left\{1,\frac{1}{u_*}
\sup_{t>0}\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\right\}.
\]
Then \(0<s(x,t)\leq M\) for all
\(x\in\overline{\Omega}\) and \(t>0\).
                                                                                                                         
On the other hand, due to  \(\Psi(1)=\Psi'(1)=0\), Taylor's formula yields
	\[
	\Psi(s)
	=\int_1^s (s-\xi)\Psi''(\xi)\,d\xi
	\geq 10M^{-6}(s-1)^2
	\qquad\mbox{for} \, \,0<s\leq M.
	\]
Therefore
\[
	E(t)=\int_\Omega\Psi(s(\cdot,t))
	\geq 10M ^{-6}\int_\Omega(s(\cdot,t)-1)^2,
	\]
	which, along with \eqref{4.21}, implies that
\eqref{4.15} holds with $\mu:=\frac{\mu_1} 2$ for all \(t>0\) after enlarging \(C\) if necessary.

title: Proof
body_md:
The estimate \eqref{1.10} follows from Lemma \ref{lemma4.4}.
To prove \eqref{1.11a}, let \(1\le p<\infty\). By Lemma \ref{lem4.5},
there exist \(C>0\) and \(\mu>0\) such that
\[
\left\|u(\cdot,t)-\frac{a}{b}\right\|_{L^2(\Omega)}
\le C e^{-\mu t}.
\]
If \(1\le p<2\), H\"{o}lder's inequality gives
\[
\left\|u(\cdot,t)-\frac{a}{b}\right\|_{L^p(\Omega)}
\le |\Omega|^{1/p-1/2}
\left\|u(\cdot,t)-\frac{a}{b}\right\|_{L^2(\Omega)}
\le C_p e^{-\mu t}.
\]
If \(2\le p<\infty\), Theorem \ref{theorem1.1} and interpolation yield
\[
\left\|u(\cdot,t)-\frac{a}{b}\right\|_{L^p(\Omega)}
\le \left\|u(\cdot,t)-\frac{a}{b}\right\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}^{1-2/p}
\left\|u(\cdot,t)-\frac{a}{b}\right\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^{2/p}
\le C_p e^{-\frac{2\mu}{p}t}.
\]
Thus \eqref{1.11a} holds with
$
\eta_p=\mu\,(1\le p<2)$, $
\eta_p=\frac{2\mu}{p}\,(p\ge2)
$.

	It remains to prove the weak-$*$ convergence in $L^\infty(\Omega)$. Set $f(t):=u(\cdot,t)-a/b$. Taking $p=1$ in \eqref{1.11a} gives
	$\|f(t)\|_{L^1(\Omega)}\to0$ as $t\to\infty$. Moreover, Theorem \ref{theorem1.1}
	provides $M>0$ such that $\|f(t)\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\leq M$ for all
	$t>0$. For any $\zeta\in L^1(\Omega)$, choose
	$\zeta_j\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ satisfying
	$\|\zeta_j-\zeta\|_{L^1(\Omega)}\to0$. Then
	\[
		\left|\int_\Omega f(t)\zeta\right|
		\leq M\|\zeta-\zeta_j\|_{L^1(\Omega)}
		+\|\zeta_j\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\|f(t)\|_{L^1(\Omega)}.
	\]
	Letting first $t\to\infty$ and then $j\to\infty$, we conclude that
	$\int_\Omega f(t)\zeta\to0$ for every $\zeta\in L^1(\Omega)$.
	This proves \eqref{1.12}.
